analysis.one_liner: Bans federal judges and Supreme Court justices from owning individual stocks, tightens their gift and recusal rules, and limits secret settlements.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the Senate, dying in the Judiciary Committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred federal judges and Supreme Court justices from owning individual stocks, banned gifts tied to privately funded judicial seminars, applied the judicial Code of Conduct to the Supreme Court for the first time, and made judges publicly disclose their conflicts. It also would have limited courts' power to seal settlements that hide information about public health or safety hazards. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received any hearing, vote, or further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who appear in federal court benefit from judges without personal financial stakes in the outcome, and consumers and workers benefit when settlements involving public health or safety hazards can no longer be sealed. Anyone who follows the Supreme Court benefits from required financial-conflict disclosures, online audio of arguments, and a complaint process for justices, who are currently the only federal judges not covered by the Code of Conduct. Court employees also gain an anonymous workplace survey covering harassment and discrimination.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Court users, litigants, and the general public

how_it_helps.text: Bans federal judges and Supreme Court justices from owning individual stocks and securities, so their rulings cannot directly affect their own portfolios.
Requires regulations restricting gifts connected to privately funded judicial seminars, closing a channel through which litigants' interests have historically paid for judges' travel and lodging.

Expresses that the Code of Conduct for U.S. Judges should apply to Supreme Court justices, who are currently the only federal judges not bound by it, and creates a committee to review complaints against the Court.

Requires judges to publicly file lists of associations and financial interests that would require them to step aside from a case, including spouses' interests, and creates a process for litigants to petition for disqualification with public written explanations.

Limits courts' ability to seal evidence and settlements in cases involving public health or safety, and bars enforcing agreements that stop parties from reporting relevant information to federal or state regulators.
Requires live online audio of appellate court arguments, public case-assignment data, easier-to-use court websites, and anonymous workplace climate surveys of court employees.

analysis.who_pays: Federal judges and Supreme Court justices pay directly: they would have to sell individual stocks, closely held businesses, and conflicted trusts, could face civil fines up to $50,000 per violation, and could no longer accept gifts connected to private seminars. Corporate defendants lose a major tool — sealed settlements and protective orders in cases involving public health or safety — and seminar sponsors lose a channel of informal access to judges.

drawbacks.text: The bill would force federal judges and Supreme Court justices to sell individual stocks and any closely held businesses, and would fine them up to $50,000 per violation — a real financial and administrative burden on judges, even with the bill's new diversified investment account as an alternative.

The proposed Supreme Court Complaints Review Committee would be appointed by House leadership and empowered to review complaints against justices and refer matters for possible impeachment, raising serious separation-of-powers questions about Congress overseeing the judicial branch — the bill itself anticipates court challenges with a severability clause.

Limits on sealing cases and settlements in cases touching public health or safety would reduce confidentiality for corporate defendants in some legitimate settlements, which defenders of current practice argue can discourage early resolution of disputes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real but hard to measure: less chance that a case is decided by a judge with money riding on the outcome, fewer junkets funded by parties with business before the courts, and less information about public health and safety buried under private settlements. The main costs are borne by the judges themselves, who would lose the right to hold individual stocks (though the bill allows them to move money into diversified funds similar to what ordinary federal employees use, and Treasury would cover administration [S3]), and some loss of confidentiality in civil settlements. The strongest good-faith objection is that parts of the bill may overreach: the Code of Conduct has always applied to lower-court judges but not the Supreme Court, and a congressional committee reviewing complaints about sitting justices raises separation-of-powers questions the bill acknowledges by including a severability clause [S3]. On balance the bill's costs fall on a small, well-off group, and its benefits run to everyone who appears in federal court.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's Judiciary Committee never took the bill up after it was referred, and it expired when the two-year congressional session ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 10, 2022, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee — the only action it ever received.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote was ever scheduled before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, which kills any bill not passed by both chambers.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal judges and Supreme Court justices keep their current stock-ownership, gift, and recusal rules, and companies that rely on sealed settlements and privately funded judicial seminars keep the status quo.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Judicial Ethics and Anti-Corruption Act of 2022 in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Wyden, Markey, Sanders, Merkley, Padilla, and Smith
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no additional senators signed on afterward.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (Chair Dick Durbin)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 10, 2022 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken on the bill; all seven original sponsors were Democrats or allied independents and no Republican cosponsored, but no party bloc acted against it on the record either.

industries.industry: Federal judges and Supreme Court justices
industries.note: Judges would have to divest individual stocks, closely held businesses, and conflicted trusts, with civil fines up to $50,000 per violation, and would lose the gift-funded seminar travel and self-judged recusal practices they currently enjoy. The bill does cushion this by letting them move money into a diversified Treasury-run account and permitting widely held index funds.

industries.industry: Corporate defendants in product and safety litigation
industries.note: The bill would restrict courts from sealing discovery and settlements in cases involving public health or safety, and from enforcing agreements that bar parties from telling regulators — removing a tool companies use to keep safety evidence out of public view and out of future lawsuits.

industries.industry: Sponsors of privately funded judicial seminars
industries.note: Gift rules would bar soliciting or accepting gifts connected to private judicial seminars — the resort courses funded by companies and foundations with business before the courts — replacing them with a small taxpayer-paid Judicial Education Fund.
